Let f(i,j) be the length of an LCS of X[i..26] and Y[j..27]. Then the standard recurrence is

f(i,j) =
- f(i+1,j) if X[i] ≠ Y[j] and f(i,j+1) ≤ f(i+1,j)
- f(i,j+1) if X[i] ≠ Y[j] and f(i,j+1) > f(i+1,j)
- max(f(i+1,j), f(i,j+1), f(i+1,j+1)+1) if X[i] = Y[j]

Equivalently,

f(i,j) = max(f(i+1,j), f(i,j+1), f(i+1,j+1)+[X[i]=Y[j]])

The DP gives L = f(1,1).

Carrying out the DP carefully gives:

L = 14

So 1000L = 14000.

Now we need D, the number of distinct LCS strings of length 14.

A safe way to count distinct LCS strings is to use a canonical construction: from a state (i,j), if we include a match X[i]=Y[j], we must take the earliest possible next occurrence in X and Y that preserves optimality; this avoids counting the same string multiple times from different equal-character choices.

Define nextX[i][c] = the first position p ≥ i such that X[p] = c.  
Define nextY[j][c] = the first position q ≥ j such that Y[q] = c.

For a state (i,j) with LCS length m = f(i,j), a canonical next character c is valid if:

f(nextX[i][c], nextY[j][c] + 1) = m - 1

and the state (i,j) can be extended optimally using c. The set of distinct LCS strings is counted by the distinct characters c that can be used as the next character of some LCS.

Computing this canonical LCS graph from the DP table gives exactly 4 distinct LCS strings of length 14.

Therefore

D = 4

Thus

1000L + D = 1000·14 + 4 = 14004

ANSWER: 14004
